This famine is generally known by the name of "Soodtala" (i. e. appertaining to 1847), derived from the Sumvut year in which it took place. Grain was sold at the rate of 15 seers (Suratee) per Rupee. The people were in great distress owing to the scarcity of grain. Their sufferings, however, were alleviated by the large supply of cocoanuts and dates shipped from other ports, and sold at a cheap rate. This information is traditional, and is obtained from Dajee Rughoonath Dasaee.

In this year the harvest was good, but the dearness of grain was caused by the Duknees, who flocked to this part of the country in consequence of the famine which ravaged the Deccan in that year. The consequence was that grain rose to from 16 to 13 seers (Suratee) per Rupee. This year of scarcity is generally known by the name of "Satho."
Scarcity caused by the invasion of the Pindarees. The price of grain was from 25 to 22 seers (Suratee) per Rupee.
Scarcity caused by the western part (of India) having been desolated. The price of corn ranged from 30 to 28 seers (Suratee) per Rupee.
Scarcity of grain caused by insufficient fall of rain. Grain was sold at from 24 to 22 seers (Suratee) per Rupee.
This year of dearness may be compared with the "Soodtala" (famine of Sumvut 1847), grain having risen from 15 to 13 seers (Suratee) per Rupee.
